title: Kepler’s Ellipses
objective: After this level you can state Kepler’s laws in plain words and explain why planets speed up near the Sun.
summary: Using Tycho Brahe’s data, Kepler found that orbits are ellipses, planets speed up near the Sun, and outer planets take longer.

cards.headline: Planets don’t move in circles. Proving it took the best data of the age.
cards.body: Copernicus kept perfect circles, and they never quite fit. Fixing that took years of careful sky-watching and one very stubborn mathematician.

cards.headline: Ellipses, not circles
cards.body: Johannes Kepler worked from the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, the best data of the age. Circles never quite matched them. Ellipses did. His first law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center. Picture a slightly squashed hoop with the Sun sitting off to one side. Not perfect, just right.

cards.headline: Faster when closer
cards.body: His second law says a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In plain terms: a planet moves fastest when it's closest to the Sun and slowest when farthest, like a skateboarder who's quickest at the bottom of the ramp. Earth is closest in early January (Level 5), so that's when it moves fastest. His third law adds that the farther out a planet orbits, the longer its year.
cards.callout: Law 2: faster near the Sun · Law 3: farther = longer year

cards.headline: Kepler’s laws: learned
learned: Kepler used Tycho Brahe’s precise observations
Law 2: planets move fastest near the Sun
Law 3: farther planets take longer to orbit

questions.prompt: What shape did Kepler find planetary orbits to be?
questions.explanation: Kepler’s first law: each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.

questions.prompt: According to Kepler’s second law, when does a planet move fastest?

options.label: When it is farthest from the Sun
When it is halfway around
options.rationale: Speed changes with distance, not with position in the year.

options.label: It always moves at the same speed
options.rationale: Its speed changes along an elliptical orbit.

options.label: When it is closest to the Sun

questions.explanation: Sweeping equal areas in equal times means the planet must move faster when it’s near the Sun.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. By Kepler’s second law, what follows?

options.label: Earth moves fastest along its orbit in January
Northern winter becomes the warmest season
options.rationale: Distance isn’t what sets the seasons.

options.label: Earth spins fastest on its axis in January
options.rationale: Kepler’s law is about orbital speed, not spin.

options.label: The Moon moves closest to Earth in January
options.rationale: The law applies to Earth orbiting the Sun.

questions.explanation: A planet moves fastest nearest the Sun. Earth is closest in early January, so that’s when it moves fastest along its orbit.
